youtube.title: Everybody jump | Possibility Lab No. 005
youtube.caption:
Would the Earth move? If all of us jumped, at once.

It sounds like it should knock the planet off course. But the push is shared out by weight, and the Earth outweighs all of us 10 trillion times over. So yes, the Earth moves when we jump. It just never notices.

Series: Season 1: Impossible, worked out, part 5 of 6.

Sources
1. A jump is a push against the ground; by Newton's third law the ground (the Earth) is pushed the other way with an equal force. — HyperPhysics: http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/conmo.html
2. About 8.2 billion people were alive in mid-2024. — un.org: https://www.un.org/development/desa/pd/world-population-prospects-2024
3. A standing jump that raises the body 0.40 m keeps it in the air 0.57 s (t = 2·sqrt(2h/g)); while the people rise, the Earth moves the opposite way so the shared centre of mass stays put. — topendsports.com: https://www.topendsports.com/testing/norms/vertical-jump.htm
4. 8.2 billion people at 62 kg is 5.1e+11 kg; the Earth is 5.97 × 10^24 kg, 1.2e+13 times more: about ten trillion (10^13) times. — NASA: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html
5. The Earth's shift is N·m·h/M = 3.4e-14 m (shown '≈ 3 × 10^-14 m'); a hydrogen atom is about 2 Bohr radii, 1.06e-10 m, across: 3,108 times wider, said as three thousand. — NIST: https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?bohrrada0

Narration: synthetic voice (AI). Animation: code-rendered, no stock footage. Every number is checked against the sources.

Possibility Lab: Impossible questions, honest assumptions, real calculations.
